meta.title: Generalized Hawking-Page transitions
meta.abstractHtml: We construct holographic backgrounds that are dual by the AdS/CFT correspondence to Euclidean conformal field theories on products of spheres , for conformal field theories whose dual may be approximated by classical Einstein gravity (typically these are large strongly coupled theories). For these backgrounds correspond to thermal field theories on , and Hawking and Page found that there are several possible bulk solutions, with two different topologies, that compete with each other, leading to a phase transition as the relative size of the spheres is modified. By numerically solving the Einstein equations we find similar results also for , with bulk solutions in which either one or the other sphere shrinks to zero smoothly at a minimal value of the radial coordinate, and with a first order phase transition (for ) between solutions of two different topologies as the relative radius changes. For a critical ratio of the radii there is a (sub-dominant) singular solution where both spheres shrink, and we analytically analyze the behavior near this radius. For the number of solutions grows to infinity as the critical ratio is approached.

children.title: Abstract
children.body: We construct holographic backgrounds that are dual by the AdS/CFT correspondence to Euclidean conformal field theories on products of spheres , for conformal field theories whose dual may be approximated by classical Einstein gravity (typically these are large strongly coupled theories). For these backgrounds correspond to thermal field theories on , and Hawking and Page found that there are several possible bulk solutions, with two different topologies, that compete with each other, leading to a phase transition as the relative size of the spheres is modified. By numerically solving the Einstein equations we find similar results also for , with bulk solutions in which either one or the other sphere shrinks to zero smoothly at a minimal value of the radial coordinate, and with a first order phase transition (for ) between solutions of two different topologies as the relative radius changes. For a critical ratio of the radii there is a (sub-dominant) singular solution where both spheres shrink, and we analytically analyze the behavior near this radius. For the number of solutions grows to infinity as the critical ratio is approached.

Gauge/gravity duality allows us to translate results in gravity to results in field theory, and vice versa. In particular, there is a large set of examples of -dimensional conformal field theories (CFTs) whose dual is well-approximated by classical Einstein gravity on (times some compact manifold). These include the large supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory at strong ‘t Hooft coupling, and the large maximally supersymmetric and CFTs. For these theories classical computations in gravity can teach us about the behavior of the field theory (in the large limit). Moreover, since the gravitational sector is shared between many different field theories (which differ, for instance, in the choice of compact manifold), gravity computations give us universal results that are valid for many different field theories.

gist.html: Classical Einstein gravity computes large $N$ strongly coupled CFTs, and its answers hold for many theories at once.

children.body: CFTs on some manifold are dual by the AdS/CFT correspondence to gravitational theories on asymptotically anti-de Sitter (AdS) spaces, whose boundary is conformally equivalent to . The most studied examples are or , where the metric is exactly anti-de Sitter. Not many results are known about other spaces (see, for instance, [1, 2, 3] for some general comments). One particularly interesting example is the Euclidean space , first studied by Hawking and Page [4]. This is interesting because it corresponds to the CFT on at finite temperature. Hawking and Page showed that there are two classes of smooth solutions with these boundary conditions. One set of solutions is given by anti-de Sitter space in global coordinates with Euclidean time identified; in this solution the factor shrinks to zero in the interior of space, such that the topology is . The other set is described by Euclidean black holes, in which the shrinks to zero in the interior at the Euclidean horizon; this set has the topology . The AdS/CFT correspondence identifies the partition function of the Euclidean field theory, in the gravity approximation, with the exponent of minus the Euclidean gravitational action (summed over all solutions with given boundary conditions). Hawking and Page showed that different classical solutions dominate the partition function at different temperatures (different ratios of the radius to the radius), with a phase transition between them at some critical temperature. When the dual field theory is a gauge theory, this phase transition may be identified (using various order parameters) with a confinement/deconfinement transition [5, 6]. On the field theory side, a sharp phase transition at finite volume is possible only when the number of degrees of freedom is infinite; for a finite number we expect a crossover. The translation of this to the gravity side is that quantum effects (corresponding to corrections in the field theory) will turn the phase transition into a crossover.

gist.html: On $S^{d-1}\times S^1$ thermal AdS and the Euclidean black hole compete; at large $N$ the switch is sharp.

children.title: The gravitational path integral and its saddles
children.body: In AdS/CFT the CFT partition function on a Euclidean manifold equals a path integral of gravity over all metrics whose conformal boundary is that manifold. When the bulk is weakly curved and Newton's constant is small, the path integral is dominated by its classical solutions, the saddles, each contributing $e^{-I/16\pi G_N}$ with $I$ its renormalized action. For a large $N$ CFT, $1/G_N$ grows like a power of $N$, so the saddle of least action wins by an exponentially large factor. Saddles can differ in topology, since only the boundary is fixed: a factor of the boundary can be filled in by a ball in the interior or kept as a sphere. When two saddles exchange the role of least action as a boundary parameter varies, the free energy has a kink, a phase transition. At finite $N$ both saddles contribute, and the kink is smoothed. The paper follows these saddles on a boundary of two spheres.

In this paper we generalize the discussion of Hawking and Page to CFTs on . This no longer has a thermal interpretation, but the CFT partition function on such Euclidean manifolds is still an interesting observable. Similar observables are computed analytically using localization in supersymmetric CFTs [7]. The result may also be related by analytic continuation to the physics of the canonical vacuum state in the CFT on the -dimensional de Sitter space times  [8]. For this case we also find that there are two possible topologies, and , and that there is a phase transition between them as the ratio of radii, is varied. We were not able to find analytical solutions for general , but we find numerical solutions for various values of ; the large isometry group of the space implies that the equations of motion are ordinary differential equations in a single variable. One important difference from the case is that here only one solution exists for and for ; there is no analog of the thermal AdS solution that exists for all ratios. In addition, there is in this case a solution with a conical singularity where both spheres shrink together, for some critical ratio . This solution can be found analytically, and we can also analyze analytically the small fluctuations around it. For we find oscillatory behavior of these fluctuations, such that the number of solutions with a given ratio grows as ; however, the new solutions and the singular solution never dominate, and there is a first order phase transition between the solution which exists at and the solution (of the other topology) which exists at , at some critical close to . The case of is unphysical, since there are no consistent quantum gravitational theories that have such solution with small curvature (indeed, even without requiring a gravity dual, there are so far no known interacting conformal field theories with ). However, the classical analysis can be performed also in this case, and leads to a second order phase transition at , with only one solution existing for every value of .

gist.html: On two spheres, solutions multiply near a cone for $d<9$, yet a single first order transition remains.

children.body: The phase structure of the Hawking-Page case, and of the case with , are schematically summarized in figure 1. The case of a CFT on was already studied by the same methods in [8], with the motivation of continuing the sphere to de Sitter space, and understanding thermal phase transitions in de Sitter space for confining theories arising from CFTs on . The results we find for the phase structure exactly agree with theirs. As in the case of the Hawking-Page transition, quantum effects should turn the phase transition into a crossover, bu we do not discuss them here.

gist.html: The phase structure agrees exactly with earlier work on $S^2\times S^d$; quantum effects, not studied, would smooth it.

children.body: We begin in section 2 by describing the setup and the observables we can compute. In section 3 we discuss in detail the singular solution and the perturbations around it. In section 4 we present some details of our numerical implementation of the holographic renormalization which is needed for computing the Euclidean action. Our numerical results are presented in section 5 for the specific case of , and then in section 6 we briefly present the results for some other representative examples.

The topology of space is different on the two sides of the phase transition, but in the pure gravity theory there is no simple order parameter that distinguishes them. If our bulk gravity theory contains -dimensional extended objects which can end on the boundary, then these correspond to -dimensional extended operators in the CFT; for example, this happens for when we have a string theory in the bulk, and strings ending on the boundary may be identified with Wilson loops. In such a case, the expectation value of the -dimensional operator integrated on gives an order parameter for the phase transition, since one can find -dimensional extended configurations in the bulk that end on the , leading to a non-zero expectation value, if and only if the topology is of the form . A similar discussion applies with . In many examples of the AdS/CFT correspondence such order parameters exist, but their field theory interpretation depends on the specific case, and we will not discuss it here.

gist.html: Pure gravity has no simple order parameter; bulk extended objects ending on a sphere would supply one.

children.body: Our results give a universal behavior for all theories that are well-approximated by classical Einstein gravity in some limit. We consider solutions where only the gravitational field is turned on, and no other fields. Assuming that all other fields are set to zero at the boundary, it is natural to expect that they will vanish in the minimal-action solutions, but this may not be true in some examples, in which case our solutions would be sub-leading saddle points in these examples.

gist.html: Only the metric is on, so the solutions are universal, though other fields may lower the action in specific theories.

children.body: In many cases it is interesting to turn on additional bulk fields in addition to the metric. In particular, for supersymmetric theories, it is often interesting to compactify them on in a way that preserves supersymmetry, and this requires turning on additional fields. In this paper we discuss only solutions with no extra fields; in particular in supersymmetric theories, these solutions preserve no supersymmetry (since it is broken by the compactification of the field theory on , in the absence of extra background fields). It would be interesting to look for solutions in which extra fields are turned on. There are also many other generalizations of our work, to different space-times, with products of more spheres, or with smaller isometry groups.

gist.html: No extra fields means no supersymmetry; supersymmetric compactifications, more spheres or less symmetry are left for later.

children.body: It would also be interesting to investigate other field theories, that do not have a dual described by classical Einstein gravity. These can include weakly coupled field theories, whose partition function can be computed in perturbation theory, and it would be interesting to compare their qualitative behavior to the one that we find here for strongly coupled field theories (for the case, a similar transition exists at large also in weakly coupled gauge theories [9, 10]).

gist.html: Weakly coupled theories on two spheres could be compared; on a sphere times a circle they show a similar transition.
On two spheres, as on a sphere times a circle, two bulk topologies compete; near the cone, solutions multiply.

brief.html: For a holographic CFT on a sphere at finite temperature, Hawking and Page found two competing bulk geometries, with a sharp transition at large $N$. Replacing the time circle by a second sphere removes the thermal meaning but keeps the competition. At extreme ratios only one topology exists, a first order transition lies between them, and for $d<9$ solutions multiply near a singular cone. Only the metric is turned on, so the picture is universal, though not necessarily dominant in every theory.

Namely, we look for -dimensional manifolds that satisfy the (Euclidean) Einstein equations with a negative cosmological constant , and have a conformal boundary . We assume for simplicity that no additional fields are turned on except the metric; this gives us universal solutions that are present in all CFTs of this type, though they may not necessarily be the dominant solutions for specific CFTs. children.title: Symmetry and ordinary differential equations
children.body: A metric invariant under the rotations $SO(d_1+1)\times SO(d_2+1)$ of both spheres has, at each point, an orbit that is a copy of $S^{d_1}\times S^{d_2}$, with only the two radii free to vary. The space is then foliated by these orbits along a single transverse direction, so the metric is fixed by functions of one variable: the radii $f$ and $h$, plus a radial component that a choice of coordinate sets to one. Einstein's equations, partial differential equations in general, become ordinary differential equations in that variable, with one constraint from the radial equation. Such geometries are called cohomogeneity one, and the reduction is the same that makes the Schwarzschild solution easy. The price is an assumption: solutions that break the symmetry are not considered, which the paper expects, without proof, to have higher action.

As in the Hawking-Page transition, we expect the solutions where space ends smoothly at to associate with two types of topologies – and . Because the entire discussion is symmetric in , it is enough to conisder the case of . In this case the sphere shrinks to zero size at (), .

gist.html: Smooth solutions have one sphere shrinking in the interior; by symmetry only $\mathbb{R}^{d_1+1}\times S^{d_2}$ need be studied.

children.title: The Fefferman–Graham expansion and the holographic stress tensor
children.body: Near the boundary of an asymptotically AdS space one can always choose coordinates with $ds^2=(d\rho^2+g_{ij}(x,\rho)dx^idx^j)/\rho^2$. Solving Einstein's equations order by order in $\rho$ gives the Fefferman–Graham expansion: the boundary metric $g_{(0)}$ fixes $g_{(2)}$ and every coefficient up to order $\rho^d$ locally, and in even $d$ a logarithmic term appears there. The coefficient $g_{(d)}$ is not fixed by the near-boundary equations; it is set by regularity deep in the interior, so it carries the information about which solution was chosen. Holographically $g_{(0)}$ is the source, the CFT metric, and $g_{(d)}$ the response: up to a constant and local terms it is the expectation value of the CFT stress tensor. The same expansion is what holographic renormalization uses to cancel the divergences of the action. The paper uses both: it reads the stress tensor off $g_{(d)}$ and integrates the action near the boundary analytically.

In the AdS/CFT correspondence, such solutions describe CFTs on a space conformally equivalent to . In our case the CFT metric is defined up to conformal transformations by the ratio between the two spheres’ radii. In terms of the bulk metric it is

(2.11)

Note that in the case of (Hawking-Page), has the interpretation of the inverse temperature of the thermal CFT on the unit sphere . Given a solution with some we can compute , which tells us which theory our saddle-point metric corresponds to.

gist.html: The boundary ratio of radii $\beta$ labels the CFT geometry; for a circle it is the inverse temperature.

children.body: In order to find the phase diagram of the theory we need to find all the saddle-point metrics with the same asymptotic geometry . We can label the solution by the triad . This label is not unique since several solutions (corresponding to different ’s) might have the same asymptotic . Moreover, in this notation a solution with a triad also has the same asymptotic geometry, and all those solutions are saddle points of the same path integral. Therefore properties of the theory should be compared between all solutions with triads of both kinds (if they exist).

gist.html: Several $r_0$ may share one $\beta$, and solutions closing either sphere must be compared at the same geometry.

children.body:
In the AdS/CFT correspondence, the partition function of the CFT may be approximated as , where is the Euclidean action of the saddle point metric2. In order to calculate it, one needs to regularize the naive Hilbert-Einstein action by introducing a boundary at some cutoff and subtracting covariant boundary counter-terms,

(2.12)

where is the metric induced on the boundary [11]. In general we need to sum the contributions to from different saddle points; in the large limit the actions are very large so we can ignore any subleading saddle points. Given an asymptotic geometry, the free energy (defined as minus the log of the partition function) is the minimum between the actions of all the different configurations with either or . We denote this function by , and it encodes the different phases of the CFT. In the case of , after dividing by , this quantity is just the thermal free energy as a function of the inverse temperature.

gist.html: The free energy $I(\beta)$ is the least renormalized Euclidean action among all solutions with that boundary.
Symmetry reduces the problem to ODEs in one radial variable; each solution is fixed by topology and closing radius $r_0$.

brief.html: Assuming the bulk keeps both spheres' symmetry, the Einstein equations become ordinary differential equations for the two sphere radii along one radial coordinate. Regularity where one sphere shrinks leaves one free number, the other sphere's closing radius $r_0$, so a topology and $r_0$ fix the solution. Its boundary ratio of radii $\beta$ says which CFT it describes, and several solutions may share it. The free energy is the least renormalized action among them, and the stress tensor is read from the boundary expansion.

children.body: Some qualitative properties of the phase diagram are apparent without calculation. In the limit , where at the boundary, we expect the smaller sphere to shrink much before the larger one, such that the only solution would have the topology with a large .3 We also expect the CFT on such a space to behave like some -dimensional theory on , which is obtained by KK reduction on the other sphere. Thus, to first order the action should scale like the normalized volume of , which is . Symmetrically, for the solution will be topologically with a large , and the action will scale like . So for both the action diverges, each limit as a result of a different bulk topology. Consequently, at least one phase transition is expected between the two topologies. Naively one may expect that decreasing decreases the asymptotic radius of the corresponding sphere, until some critical radius where , where this branch of solutions connects to the branch with the other topology. In this case there would be just a single solution for every radius in the CFT, and a smooth transition between the two branches at . We will see that this is true when , but not in the physically interesting range of dimensions , where the asymptotic radius will not be monotonic in . In this range more than one solution of the same topology can exist for the same asymptotic radii. Recall that this happens already for , where both “large” and “small” AdS black holes can exist with the same temperature.

gist.html: Each extreme ratio has one topology with diverging action, so at least one transition must occur between them.

children.title: Kol's double cone and complex exponents
children.body: A cone over a product of spheres, $ds^2=dr^2+r^2(a^2d\Omega_m^2+b^2d\Omega_n^2)$, is Ricci-flat for $a^2=(m-1)/(m+n-1)$ and $b^2=(n-1)/(m+n-1)$. Kol proposed such a double cone, over $S^2\times S^{D-3}$, as the local geometry where a black string pinches into a black hole, a point at which the topology changes. Linear deformations of a cone are power laws, $r^s$, since the cone has no scale. In $D$ spacetime dimensions the exponents are $s=-\tfrac12\big(D-2\pm\sqrt{(D-2)(D-10)}\big)$, real for $D\ge10$ and complex below. Complex exponents mean deformations that oscillate in $\log r$, so families of solutions approaching the cone spiral rather than arrive monotonically; $D=10$ is a critical dimension. Kalisch, Möckel and Ammon later studied this critical behaviour numerically. Near its tip, where $\sinh z\approx z$, the paper's singular solution is such a cone, with $D=d+1$, so $d<9$ is the oscillating case.

For each such solution we can find the change in the asymptotic ratio of radii (2.11); using (3.8) we find at first order in :

children.title: Log-periodic oscillations and multiplying solutions
children.body: Suppose a boundary quantity behaves along a family of solutions as $\beta-\beta_s\propto r_0^{p}\cos(\omega\log r_0+\phi)$. As $r_0\to0$ these are log-periodic oscillations: each step of $\pi/\omega$ in $\log r_0$ crosses $\beta_s$ once more, with a turning point between crossings, and the amplitude shrinks geometrically. A value of $\beta$ near $\beta_s$ is then met by the family many times, more the closer it is, so the number of solutions grows without bound, multiplying roughly as $\log(1/|\beta-\beta_s|)$. Plotted against a second quantity that oscillates with another phase, the family traces a spiral. Along the family the action is stationary under variations at fixed boundary, so at each turning point of $\beta$ the curve $I(\beta)$ has a cusp, as for small and large AdS black holes at their minimum temperature. Which branch dominates is then decided by the sign of the action's second-order change, which the paper settles numerically.

From the analysis above we can draw a schematic picture of the phase map (figure 1). Around the action diverges like respectively (we take ), each divergence comes from a different bulk topology. The two branches coincide at and at the same action. From (3.10) we expect decayed oscillations of toward as . Because (3.14), the two topologies approach in with zero slope. The minimal action curve is expected to have at least one first order phase transition, close to on the axis (see figure 1). Note that the second order variation of the action with respect to the deviation from the singular solution dictates whether there will be an infinite amount of phase transitions, which would happen if the action decreases as the solution becomes singular. In figure 1 we assumed that the action increases, so that we get a single first order phase transition; this scenario will be confirmed by our numerical analysis. Finally, by (3.13) oscillates in a similar fashion to the ratio of radii but with (presumably) different phase and amplitude. Therefore the function is expected to have spiral behavior around the point .

gist.html: Both branches reach $\beta_s$ with zero slope; if the action rises towards the cone, one first order transition results.

An exact cone at $\beta_s$ organises the solutions: for $d<9$ they spiral into it, giving infinitely many.

brief.html: At extreme ratios one topology exists, with diverging action, so a transition must occur in between. At $r_0=0$ an exact singular solution, a cone where both spheres shrink together, exists at $\beta_s=\sqrt{(d_2-1)/(d_1-1)}$. Smooth solutions with small $r_0$ are linear deformations of it, and for $d<9$ their exponent is complex: $\beta$ approaches $\beta_s$ in oscillations decaying as $r_0^{(d-1)/2}$, so solutions multiply. The action is stationary at the cone, so both branches arrive with zero slope. For $d\ge9$ the approach is monotonic, suggesting a second order transition.

children.body: In order to find solutions for general (general ) we take initial conditions with many different values of , and numerically solve the differential equations (2.6).

gist.html: Solutions for general $\beta$ come from integrating the ODEs for many closing radii $r_0$.

children.body:
Given a numerical solution for the equations of motion (2.6) we would like to calculate its Euclidean action. As mentioned above (2.12), the Hilbert-Einstein action should be regularized and renormalized by local boundary counter terms in order to be finite. The expression for the action is

(4.1)

where (for ) [11]

In (4.2) the metric is at the point , whereas in (4.3) (and the curvatures in the integrand) is the induced metric from on the sub-manifold at . Each term in (4.3) appears only for high enough dimension. The first appears for any , the second for and the third for . The counter-terms remove the diverging part of the regularized action, so that the limit of (4.1) gives a finite answer.

gist.html: Counter-terms at a cutoff surface make the Euclidean action finite as the cutoff is removed.

children.body:
Unfortunately, a naive numerical calculation of (4.1) leads to a significant numerical error arising from the subtraction of two large and close numbers. One possible solution is to write the sum using one integrand. Defining , we obtain

(4.4)

The new integrand opens up a different problem: might diverge (depending on ) around the closing point . For this reason we use the fact that both integrands are finite in the bulk, and write instead

(4.5)

where was chosen such that the first and last terms are comparably small. Although this solution reduces the error around the boundary, it is not enough to eliminate it to a sufficient degree. Close to the boundary the two integrands (of the first integral in (4.5)) diverge differently, and so the complete integral still carries a large numerical error in the limit . Nonetheless, we can trust the value of the numerical integral (4.5) for which is not too small.

gist.html: Subtracting counter-terms numerically cancels large numbers; one integrand helps but still errs near the boundary.

children.body:
To find the value of with better accuracy we can incorporate the Fefferman-Graham expansion of around (2.9),(2.10). We can expand the integrand of the renormalized action up to some positive power of as a local functional of (the entire expansion of the function in (2.8) may be written using local functionals of ). Taking the integral between and will give the correct up to the positive power . We can denote it . This expression is still a local function of . Their value can be found numerically by fitting the numerical solution in some range between and some small to the analytical expansion of the metric, up to the positive order . The combined calculation of the action can be written as

(4.6)

We note that there is a trade-off in choosing . Making it too small will bring back the numerical error caused by the integrands’ divergence in (4.5). Making it too large will result in a larger error in , as it was calculated with error .

gist.html: Near the boundary the action is integrated analytically from a fitted Fefferman–Graham expansion, numerically beyond.

children.body:
In the convention we chose for the coordinates (2.8) the solution’s closing point is at . Choosing a different closing point is equivalent to taking a different boundary metric , related by a conformal transformation. For even dimensions, due to the conformal anomaly, this choice affects the action, so we need to fix it when comparing different solutions. We will choose our CFT coordinates such that the total CFT volume is constant, independent of . Our numerical solutions generally give a different volume, and to fix this we use the transformation . The scale anomaly , which is non zero only for even dimensions, is known analytically as a local functional of the boundary metric  [14]. We thus need to add an extra factor

(4.7)


and this gives our final result which we plot below. Note that the additional terms ensures that we still have (3.14) at leading order in the deviation away from the singular solution.

gist.html: In even dimensions the conformal anomaly makes the action frame-dependent, so the CFT volume is fixed.

children.body:
Several arbitrary parameters were introduced above to carry out the calculation of the action. Here is a list with the explanation of each of them, together with the measured effect of altering their value.

  • - used to specify the range of integration for the counter-terms (4.5). Varying has almost no effect on the final result.

  • - the range from which the fit to the analytical expansion, determining and , was taken. Varying has almost no effect on the final result.

  • - circumscribes between the analytical and the numerical integration. needed some fine-tuning, to minimize the numerical errors.

The figures we draw below contain estimates of the numerical errors, though in most cases these are too small to be visible. These can be reduced by increasing the accuracy of the numerical analysis.

gist.html: Two of the three numerical parameters barely matter; the matching point needs tuning, and error bars are mostly invisible.
The renormalized action is computed analytically near the boundary and numerically beyond, with the CFT volume held fixed.

brief.html: The renormalized action is a difference of large numbers near the boundary, which a direct numerical integral handles badly. The method therefore fits the numerical metric near the boundary to its Fefferman–Graham expansion, integrates that strip analytically and the rest numerically. In even dimensions the conformal anomaly makes the action depend on the conformal frame, so all solutions are compared at fixed CFT volume. Only the matching point needs tuning.

children.body: As we described in section 2, for a given CFT metric we need to consider all the bulk solutions with that boundary metric. We now label the CFT geometry by the ratio of the radius to the radius, where . Note that in the notations of section 2 we need to consider solutions both with a closed sphere and ratio , and with a closed sphere and ratio . In the case of we can consider the same solution under both and . In this section we will describe the features found in the numerical analysis for various through the example of . Some plots for other dimensions are given in the next section.

gist.html: Solutions closing either sphere, at ratio $\beta$ or $1/\beta$, are compared; $S^3\times S^2$ serves as the example.

children.body: The analytical examination above (section 3) suggests that for large the open sphere in the IR would stay bigger along the bulk, and the final ratio of radii would be very large or very small (depending on the convention for the ratio). For small a complex critical exponent was predicted near (3.3). In figure 2 we can see exactly those characteristics. Similar behavior can be found also for other (see section 6). The analytical description captures all the qualitative features appearing in the figures.

gist.html: Large closing radii give extreme ratios and small ones oscillate about $\beta_s$, as the analysis predicted.

children.body: The behavior of around the singular solution was found above to take the form where and . In order to check this result we fitted the log of the calculated to the aforementioned equation, to find . The fit was taken with the function FindFit of Mathematica with 100 data points, for between and (which is also the lower bound for accurate results of using the Mathematica integrator). The results are presented in table 1. The numerical exponent agrees with the analytical one to high precision. It is evident that the error in the fit grows with the total dimension . This is because the frequency becomes smaller as gets closer to , making it more difficult to estimate it over the same data range. As expected, no oscillations were found for (not shown in the table).

gist.html: Fitted exponents match the prediction, less well as $d$ nears 9; for $d\ge9$ no oscillations appear.

brief.html: Large closing radii give extreme ratios of radii, and small ones make $\beta$ oscillate into the singular value, on both branches. Fitting $\beta(r_0)-\beta_s$ for $r_0$ between $e^{-7}$ and $e^{-1}$ recovers the predicted decay rate $(d-1)/2$ and frequency $\tfrac12\sqrt{(d-1)(9-d)}$, with errors growing as $d$ approaches 9, where the frequency falls. No oscillations appear for $d\ge9$.

children.body: In figure 1 we drew a schematic picture of , the action as a function of the ratio. We expect to diverge. We also expect the two topologies to approach with zero-slope decayed oscillations. In all cases, we found numerically that the action decreases at second order in the expansion around the singular solution. We haven’t found an analytical explanation for this fact. Thus the simplest scenario (like the one drawn in figure 1) would be a single first order phase transition between the two topologies, close to . Figure 3 agrees with this description and exhibits one first order phase transition. The critical ratio of the phase transition for this case agree with the results previously found in [8].

gist.html: The action is numerically found to decrease away from the cone, so a single first order transition occurs.

children.body: There are two cases that display a somewhat different behavior than that in figures 1 and 3. The first is the case of equal spheres . The behavior there is very similar besides the sign of the divergence at (we show examples of this in the next section). The second is the Hawking-Page , shown on the left-hand side of figure 1, where there are no oscillations (as there is no singular solution).

gist.html: Equal spheres differ only in the sign of the extreme-ratio action; for $S^3\times S^2$, $\beta_c=0.720$.
The action falls away from the cone, so one first order transition occurs, close to $\beta_s$.

brief.html: The action diverges at extreme ratios and the two branches reach $\beta_s$ with zero slope, as expected. In every case computed the action decreases away from the cone at second order, which the paper cannot yet explain, so the simplest scenario follows: a single first order transition, close to $\beta_s$. For $S^3\times S^2$ it lies at $\beta_c=0.720$, agreeing with earlier work; the Hawking–Page case has no oscillations, having no singular solution.

Because is traceless the two components are dependent, and it is enough to plot . Based on the analysis above, we expect around to have spiral decayed oscillations toward the singular value . In figure 4 we can see exactly this behavior. Similar behavior can be found also for other (see section 6). All the graphs display a transition between monotonic behavior at extreme ratios (), and the spiral decay around .

gist.html: The traceless stress tensor $g_{(d)}$ is monotonic at extreme ratios and spirals into zero at $\beta_s$.
The stress tensor spirals into its singular value as the ratio approaches $\beta_s$.

brief.html: The coefficient $g_{(d)}$, proportional to the traceless CFT stress tensor, is monotonic at extreme ratios. Near the singular ratio it oscillates as the ratio does, presumably with another phase and amplitude, so plotted against $\beta$ it spirals into the singular solution's value, zero, at $\beta_s$. The $S^3\times S^2$ numerics show exactly this.

gist.html: For $S^3\times S^2$ the numerics confirm the spiral and find one first order transition at $\beta_c=0.720$.

brief.html: For $S^3\times S^2$, solutions closing either sphere are compared at the same boundary geometry. The ratio of radii behaves as the analysis of the cone predicted, oscillating into $\beta_s$ with the computed exponent, more poorly resolved as $d$ nears 9. The action turns out to decrease away from the cone, a fact without analytic explanation, so the many solutions near $\beta_s$ never dominate and a single first order transition occurs, at $\beta_c=0.720$ against $\beta_s\approx0.707$. The stress tensor spirals into its singular value.

The transition sits at $\beta_c=1$, the singular ratio, where exchanging the spheres maps $\beta$ to $1/\beta$ and swaps the two topologies. There is one first order transition, at $\beta_c=0.584$, just above the singular ratio $\beta_s\approx0.577$. This phase structure agrees with earlier results by Blackman, McDermott and Van Raamsdonk.

gist.html: Equal spheres and $S^4\times S^2$ repeat the $S^3\times S^2$ picture, with one first order transition each.

brief.html: For equal spheres, $S^2\times S^2$ and $S^3\times S^3$, the picture is that of $S^3\times S^2$, with the transition at $\beta_c=1$. The one difference is the sign of the action at extreme ratios, negative for $S^2\times S^2$ and positive for $S^3\times S^3$. $S^4\times S^2$ follows $S^3\times S^2$, with a first order transition at $\beta_c=0.584$ that agrees with earlier work.

gist.html:
• Context Hawking and Page found two bulk geometries competing for a holographic CFT on a sphere at finite temperature. What if the time circle becomes a second sphere?
  • Result
    • Either sphere can shrink smoothly in the bulk; numerically, for CFT dimension $d<9$, a first order transition separates these topologies as the ratio varies.
    • At a critical ratio of radii, an exact singular solution, both spheres shrinking to a cone, is sub-dominant.
    • Near it, for $d<9$, the cone's deformations oscillate, so solutions multiply without bound.
  • Why it matters With only the metric on, this phase structure is universal for CFTs with classical Einstein duals, unless other fields lower the action.

specialist.html:
• Context Hawking and Page found thermal AdS and the black hole competing for boundary $S^{d-1}\times S^1$. For $S^{d_1}\times S^{d_2}$ the symmetric Einstein equations reduce to ODEs, but no analytic solution is found at a general ratio.
  • Result
    • Either sphere caps off smoothly at a closing radius $r_0$, with one solution at extreme ratios; for $d<9$ a first order transition lies near $\beta_s$, at $\beta_c=0.720$ for $S^3\times S^2$, agreeing with Blackman, McDermott and Van Raamsdonk.
    • The cone $f,h\propto\sinh z$ at $\beta_s=\sqrt{(d_2-1)/(d_1-1)}$ is exact and sub-dominant; its traceless deformation leaves the action unchanged at leading order, so both branches are expected to arrive with zero slope.
    • For $d<9$ the deformation exponent is complex: $\beta-\beta_s\propto r_0^{(d-1)/2}\cos(\omega\log r_0+\phi)$, confirmed by fits, so solutions multiply without bound near $\beta_s$.
  • Why it matters The two-sphere partition function is a non-thermal observable, possibly continued to de Sitter times a sphere, and these Einstein-only saddles are universal, though possibly sub-leading where other fields condense.

student.html:
• Context In holography, Hawking and Page found two spacetimes competing for a field theory on a hot sphere. What if time's circle becomes a second sphere?
  • Result
    • Numerically, either sphere can shrink smoothly to a point; if the two dimensions sum to under nine, a sudden (first order) transition separates the shapes.
    • At one critical size ratio, an exact solution has both spheres shrinking together to a singular cone; it never dominates.
    • Near that ratio, in the same dimensions, the cone's deformations oscillate, so ever more solutions appear.
  • Why it matters Only gravity enters, so this holds for theories well described by classical Einstein gravity, unless other fields interfere.

brief.html:
For a holographic CFT on a sphere at finite temperature, Hawking and Page found two competing bulk geometries. In thermal AdS the sphere shrinks to zero inside; in the Euclidean black hole the time circle does. The paper replaces the circle by a second sphere, for CFTs dual to classical Einstein gravity. The partition function on $S^{d_1}\times S^{d_2}$ is no longer thermal but is still an observable, and the answer is universal, because only the metric is turned on. Again two topologies compete, with a first order transition for CFT dimension $d<9$, and near a critical ratio of radii the number of solutions grows without bound.

Symmetry reduces the Einstein equations to ODEs along one radial direction. Space ends smoothly where one sphere shrinks, and the other sphere's radius there, the closing radius $r_0$, fixes the solution and its boundary ratio of radii $\beta$. At extreme ratios the smaller sphere shrinks first, so each extreme has a single solution of its own topology, with diverging action. Unlike thermal AdS, neither topology exists at every ratio, so the two must exchange dominance.

At $r_0=0$ both spheres shrink together to a cone. This singular solution is exact and sits at the critical ratio $\beta_s=\sqrt{(d_2-1)/(d_1-1)}$. Smooth solutions with small $r_0$ are small deformations of the cone, whose exponent is complex for $d<9$. So $\beta$ approaches $\beta_s$ in damped oscillations, $\beta-\beta_s\propto r_0^{(d-1)/2}\cos(\tfrac12\sqrt{(d-1)(9-d)}\log r_0+\phi)$, and solutions multiply near $\beta_s$. The action is stationary under this deformation, so both branches reach $\beta_s$ with zero slope. For $d\ge9$ the approach is monotonic, with one solution per ratio and, classically, a second order transition at $\beta_s$.

The renormalized action is computed by fitting the near-boundary expansion and integrating that region analytically, the interior numerically, at fixed CFT volume. Fits recover the predicted exponents, less precisely as $d$ nears 9. The action turns out to decrease away from the cone, so the extra solutions should never dominate. The numerics show the simplest scenario, a single first order transition near $\beta_s$: for $S^3\times S^2$ at $\beta_c=0.720$, against $\beta_s\approx0.707$, agreeing with earlier work. The stress tensor spirals into its singular value, and equal spheres and $S^4\times S^2$ behave alike.

Only the metric is turned on and both spheres' symmetry is assumed, so in specific theories other solutions could dominate. Quantum effects, which should turn the transition into a crossover at finite $N$, are not studied. The oscillations' amplitude and phase are only fitted, and why the action decreases away from the cone has no analytic explanation.

defs.html: Said of the solution with the least Euclidean action among all those with the given boundary: at large $N$ it alone fixes the partition function, the others being suppressed by $e^{-\Delta I/16\pi G_N}$. A sub-dominant, or sub-leading, solution exists but does not contribute at leading order.

at.quote: different classical solutions dominate the partition function

defs.html: A black hole continued to imaginary time, with time periodic so that the geometry is smooth at the horizon. There the time circle shrinks to zero, so the topology is $S^{d-1}\times\mathbb{R}^2$, and the period sets the temperature. Its action gives the black hole's free energy.

Said of a sphere whose radius goes to zero at an interior point of the bulk, where space ends. If it does so smoothly, like the origin of polar coordinates, the sphere and the radial direction fill out a ball; so which sphere shrinks fixes the topology of the solution.

at.quote: factor shrinks to zero in the interior of space

defs.html: In a large $N$ gauge theory, the change from a low-temperature phase whose free energy is of order one, made of colour singlets, to a high-temperature phase whose free energy is of order $N^2$. On a sphere it is sharp only at infinite $N$; holographically it is the Hawking–Page transition.

A smooth, possibly rapid change between two regimes, with no singularity in the free energy. In a finite volume a sharp phase transition needs infinitely many degrees of freedom, so at finite $N$ the transitions found here are expected to become crossovers, through quantum ($1/N$) effects in the bulk.

A technique that computes some supersymmetric observables exactly, such as partition functions on spheres, by deforming the path integral with a supersymmetric term until it reduces to a finite-dimensional integral. It needs a background that preserves supersymmetry, which the paper's solutions, with only the metric turned on, do not.

$\beta=R_{S^{d_2}}/R_{S^{d_1}}$, the ratio of the two boundary spheres' radii: the only parameter of the boundary geometry once overall rescalings are ignored. For $d_2=1$ it is the inverse temperature in units of the sphere's radius. Exchanging the spheres maps $\beta$ to $1/\beta$.

Global anti-de Sitter space with Euclidean time made periodic. Its boundary is $S^{d-1}\times S^1$, the sphere shrinks to zero in the interior (topology $\mathbb{R}^d\times S^1$), and it solves Einstein's equations at every temperature. On two spheres no solution exists at every ratio of radii.

A point where space looks like the tip of a cone rather than a smooth origin. Here both spheres shrink together at one point with a fixed ratio of sizes, so near it space is a cone over $S^{d_1}\times S^{d_2}$ and the curvature diverges; classical gravity cannot be trusted at the tip.

at.quote: a solution with a conical singularity

defs.html: Mostly $\beta_s=\sqrt{(d_2-1)/(d_1-1)}$, the ratio of radii at which the singular solution exists and near which solutions multiply. The paper also writes “critical ratio of the phase transition” for $\beta_c$, where the dominant topology changes; $\beta_c$ is close to $\beta_s$ but differs, $0.720$ against $0.707$ for $S^3\times S^2$.

The exact solution in which both spheres shrink together at one point, a conical singularity; both radii are proportional to $\sinh z$. It needs both spheres of dimension above one, exists only at the critical ratio $\beta_s$, and for $d<9$ never dominates.

A transition at which the free energy is continuous but its first derivative jumps: two distinct solutions cross in $I(\beta)$ and exchange dominance. In a second order transition one solution turns continuously into the other, as the paper finds classically for $d\ge9$.

at.quote: there is a first order phase transition

defs.html: The transition, found by Hawking and Page in 1983, between thermal AdS and the AdS black hole as the dominant Euclidean solution with boundary $S^{d-1}\times S^1$. Holographically it is a large $N$ phase transition of the CFT on a sphere as the temperature varies, in gauge theories a deconfinement transition.

The procedure that makes the on-shell gravitational action finite: cut space off near the boundary, add local counter-terms built from the metric induced on the cut-off surface, then remove the cutoff. It is the gravity side of renormalizing the CFT and yields finite partition functions and stress tensors.

The renormalized gravitational action of a solution in imaginary time. The CFT partition function is $Z\simeq e^{-I/16\pi G_N}$, so the solution of least action dominates. $I(\beta)$, the least action at a given ratio of radii, is the free energy; for $d_2=1$ it is $\beta$ times the thermal free energy.

A classical solution of the Euclidean equations with the given boundary. Each contributes about $e^{-I/16\pi G_N}$ to the partition function, so at large $N$ the one of least action dominates and the rest are sub-leading. Here the saddles are labelled by their topology and closing radius, plus the singular one.

The boundary at infinity of an asymptotically AdS space. The metric blows up there, so it is defined only after multiplying by a vanishing factor, and hence only up to rescaling by a function. The CFT lives on it, so only rescaling-invariant data, here the ratio of radii, label the theory.

The expansion of an asymptotically AdS metric in powers of the radial coordinate $\rho$ near the boundary, $g=g_{(0)}+\rho^2g_{(2)}+\dots+\rho^dg_{(d)}+\dots$, with a logarithm in even $d$. $g_{(0)}$ is the CFT's metric and fixes the lower terms; $g_{(d)}$ is free and gives the stress tensor.

The interior point, $z=0$ or $\rho=1$, where a sphere shrinks to zero and space ends; for the singular solution both shrink there. Regularity at it gives the initial conditions of the equations of motion, leaving only the closing radius free.

$r_0$, the radius of the sphere that stays finite at the closing point, where the other sphere shrinks. With the choice of which sphere shrinks it fixes the solution: large $r_0$ gives extreme ratios of radii, and $r_0\to0$ approaches the singular solution.

The curvature invariant $K=R_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}R^{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}$, the square of the Riemann tensor. It is finite wherever the geometry is smooth, so keeping it finite at the closing point gives the regularity conditions. It grows as $r_0^{-2}$ at small closing radius.

Here minus the logarithm of the CFT partition function on $S^{d_1}\times S^{d_2}$, given at large $N$ by $I(\beta)$, the least action among all solutions with that boundary. For $d_2=1$, divided by $\beta$, it is the thermal free energy. Its non-analyticities in $\beta$ are the phase transitions.

defs.html: Kaluza–Klein reduction: describing a theory on a small compact space, here the smaller sphere, by an effective theory in the remaining dimensions. The paper uses it to argue that at extreme ratios the CFT acts as a $d_1$-dimensional theory on the larger sphere, so the action scales as that sphere's volume.

defs.html: The deformation of the singular solution that enlarges one sphere and shrinks the other, $\delta f/f=a/d_1$ and $\delta h/h=-a/d_2$, so the volume is unchanged at first order. The only other linear deformation, with a trace, is a shift of the coordinate. The traceless one leaves the action unchanged at first order.

The exponent $\alpha$ of the power law $a\simeq z^\alpha$ obeyed by deformations of the singular solution near its tip. For $d<9$ it is complex, $\alpha=-\tfrac12\big(d-1\pm i\sqrt{(d-1)(9-d)}\big)$: its real part gives a power-law decay and its imaginary part oscillations in $\log r_0$.

In even dimensions, the failure of a CFT's partition function to be unchanged when the background metric is rescaled: under $g_{(0)}\to e^{2\sigma}g_{(0)}$ the action shifts by a local curvature density integrated against $\sigma$. So the action on two spheres depends on their overall size, which the paper therefore fixes.

questions.a: The CFT lives on $S^{d_1}\times S^{d_2}$ in $d=d_1+d_2$ dimensions; the bulk has $D=d+1$. $z$ is the radial distance from the closing point ($z\to\infty$ at the boundary) and $\rho=e^{-z}$, with the boundary at $\rho=0$. $r_0$ is the radius of the sphere that does not shrink at the closing point. $\beta$ is the boundary ratio $R_{S^{d_2}}/R_{S^{d_1}}$; $\beta_s$ is where the singular solution sits, $\beta_c$ where the dominant topology changes. The AdS radius is 1.

questions.q: Why is there no analogue of thermal AdS, which exists at every temperature?
questions.a: For $d_2=1$ global AdS with periodic Euclidean time is an exact solution for any period, because time translation is a symmetry of global AdS, so time can be identified with any period. With two spheres of dimension two or more nothing plays that role: when it is much smaller than the other at the boundary it is expected to shrink first, so at extreme ratios only one topology exists, and each extreme has a different one.

questions.q: Why study a singular solution that never dominates?
questions.a: Because it is the one solution known in closed form, and it organises all the others near it. Smooth solutions with small closing radius look like the cone away from their tip, so their behaviour follows from linear deformations of the cone: the oscillations of $\beta$, the multiplying solutions, the zero slope of the action, and the spiral of the stress tensor. The numerics then only need to settle what the linear analysis leaves open.

questions.q: Where does the critical dimension $d=9$ come from, and why is $d\ge9$ called unphysical?
questions.a: The deformation exponent is $\alpha_\pm=-\tfrac12\big(d-1\pm\sqrt{(d-1)(d-9)}\big)$, complex exactly when $d<9$; then deformations oscillate and solutions multiply, while for $d\ge9$ the ratio is monotonic in $r_0$. The case $d\ge9$ is called unphysical because no consistent quantum gravity is known with such a weakly curved $AdS_{d+1}$, and no interacting CFT is known in $d\ge9$.

questions.q: Why do both branches reach $\beta_s$ with zero slope in $I(\beta)$?
questions.a: The singular solution's boundary metric is a fixed metric times a function of $\rho$, so the first variation of the action is proportional to the trace of the change in the boundary metric. The deformation that moves $\beta$ is traceless, so the action does not change at first order while $\beta$ does. The anomaly term added in even dimensions preserves this.

questions.q: Do the infinitely many solutions near the critical ratio change the phase diagram?
questions.a: Not at leading order. Whether they matter depends on the sign of the action's second-order change away from the cone. Had the action fallen towards the cone, ever newer branches would dominate and there would be infinitely many transitions. Numerically the action is always lower away from the cone, so the outermost branches dominate and there is one first order transition, close to $\beta_s$. The paper has no analytic explanation for this sign.

questions.q: How reliable are the numerical actions and exponents?
questions.a: Errors in the action, from the near-boundary cancellation, are estimated and mostly too small to see; two of the method's parameters barely affect the result, while the matching point needed tuning. The fitted exponents match the prediction well at small $d$ but worse towards $d=8$, where the frequency is small and harder to resolve over the accessible range $e^{-7}<r_0<e^{-1}$.

questions.q: Why must the total CFT volume be fixed when comparing solutions?
questions.a: In even $d$ the conformal anomaly makes the action change under a rescaling of the boundary metric, so two solutions with the same ratio of radii but different overall size would have different actions for a trivial reason. The paper's numerical solutions come out with different volumes, so each action is corrected by the anomaly's known local term to a common, $\beta$-independent volume.

questions.q: What was known before, and does it agree?
questions.a: Hawking and Page settled $S^{d-1}\times S^1$. CFTs on $S^2\times S^d$ were studied by the same methods by Blackman, McDermott and Van Raamsdonk, aiming to continue $S^d$ to de Sitter space. The phase structure found here agrees exactly with theirs, including the critical ratios for $S^3\times S^2$ and $S^4\times S^2$. What is new is the general $S^{d_1}\times S^{d_2}$, the analysis of the singular solution, and its oscillations.

questions.q: Is there an order parameter that tells the two phases apart?
questions.a: Not in pure gravity. If the bulk theory has $(d_2+1)$-dimensional objects that can end on the boundary, they define $d_2$-dimensional operators wrapping $S^{d_2}$, and their expectation value is non-zero only if a bulk object can end on that sphere, that is, only in the topology where $S^{d_2}$ shrinks. Strings and Wilson loops are the $d_2=1$ case. The field theory meaning depends on the example and is not discussed.

questions.q: What does the paper not show?
questions.a: It turns on only the metric, so in specific theories other fields could give lower-action solutions, and supersymmetric compactifications are not studied. It assumes the bulk keeps both spheres' symmetry. Quantum effects, which should turn the transition into a crossover, are not computed. The oscillation amplitude and phase are only fitted, the sign of the second-order action is unexplained, and the weakly coupled field theory comparison is left open.

questions.q: Can the solutions be trusted near the tip of the cone?
questions.a: Not where both $r_0$ and $z$ are very small: curvature grows like $r_0^{-2}$, and higher-curvature corrections to Einstein's equations, neglected here, become important. The paper states that the features it describes do not depend on these corrections for $d<9$. For $d\ge9$, where the singular solution dominates at one ratio, they would be needed to fix the nature of the transition.
